youtube.baslik: Case: Tinnitus with a Normal Audiogram | Lesson 281 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
In a fictional adult case, we assess tinnitus that comes with a normal audiogram: red flags, DPOAEs, extended high-frequency audiometry, the concept of hidden hearing loss, a speech-in-noise test, the THI and questions about hyperacusis, a counseling plan, and follow-up with the THI.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Tunkel et al., Clinical Practice Guideline: Tinnitus (2014); McCombe et al., Guidelines for the grading of tinnitus severity (2001); Newman et al., Development of the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (1996); Jafari et al., A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Extended High-Frequency Hearing Thresholds in Tinnitus With a Normal Audiogram, Ear and Hearing (2022).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Extended high frequencies, THI and counseling
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we work through an adult case with tinnitus complaints even though the audiogram is normal.
We will cover extended high-frequency audiometry, otoacoustic emissions, questions about tinnitus and hyperacusis, and a counseling plan.

maddeler.metin: _High-pitched ringing_ in both ears, six months
Marked at night and in quiet

cumleler: Our case is fictional: a thirty-four-year-old person comes in complaining of ringing in both ears.
The tinnitus has been present for about six months; it is described as a high-pitched, constant sound in both ears.
At work during the day it is barely noticed, but it becomes very clear in bed at night and in quiet places.
The person says they have gone to concerts often for years and listened to loud music through headphones on public transport.
They have trouble falling asleep and fear that the ringing is a sign of permanent damage.
They add that they find it much harder than before to follow conversations in crowded restaurants.
In every tinnitus visit, we first ask about conditions needing a physician: tinnitus in time with the pulse, or pulsatile tinnitus.
Unilateral tinnitus matters too, especially with hearing loss or asymmetry in the same ear.
When tinnitus starts together with sudden hearing loss, time matters; these people are referred without waiting.
Vertigo, facial weakness or other neurological signs also call for a physician's assessment.
In our case none of these are present; the tinnitus is bilateral, constant and came on slowly.
Otoscopy is normal; thresholds from two hundred fifty to eight thousand hertz are within normal limits in both ears.
Word recognition scores are one hundred percent in both ears.
Tympanograms are type A, and acoustic reflexes are at expected levels.
From the standard audiogram's point of view, hearing is normal; but this does not mean the tinnitus is not real.
A normal audiogram shows only thresholds from two hundred fifty to eight thousand hertz; it does not show every function of the cochlea.

notlar.metin: Interpret with the course over time

cumleler: To assess outer hair cell function, distortion product otoacoustic emissions, or DPOAEs, were recorded.
In both ears, DPOAE responses are clearly above the noise floor in the mid frequencies.
But between four thousand and eight thousand hertz, response amplitudes are low and borderline at some frequencies.
Although thresholds are normal, this finding may suggest an early change in outer hair cell function in the high-frequency region.
OAE findings are not interpreted alone either; they are weighed with other tests and with the course over time.
Extended high-frequency audiometry measures thresholds above eight thousand hertz.
In this case thresholds rise clearly from ten thousand hertz; at fourteen thousand hertz they reach fifty to fifty-five decibels.
At sixteen thousand hertz there is no response at the audiometer's maximum output.
At these frequencies thresholds change markedly with age and norms are limited; still, this drop is marked for a thirty-four-year-old.
A meta-analysis showed that thresholds at these frequencies are worse in tinnitus patients with a normal audiogram.
This finding offers a clue to the source of the tinnitus and helps us give the person an explanation.
Another possibility is loss of the connections between inner hair cells and auditory nerve fibers; this is called cochlear synaptopathy.
Because thresholds are not affected, the audiogram looks normal; so this condition is also called hidden hearing loss.
It has been proposed that it may be linked to difficulty understanding speech in noise and to tinnitus.
But there is not yet a standard clinical test that shows this condition directly in humans; the concept is still being researched.
So we explain it to the person not as a diagnosis, but as a possible mechanism under study.
The noise exposure history in our case is one of the reasons this possibility comes to mind.
Because of difficulty in crowds, the QuickSIN test was done; the signal-to-noise ratio, or SNR, loss is four decibels.
According to the test manual, three to seven decibels is a mild SNR loss.
With a score of one hundred percent in quiet, a mild loss in noise fits the person's complaint about restaurants.
This measurement is recorded as a baseline for comparing change at follow-up.
Speech-in-noise tests are one way to put numbers on everyday complaints in people with normal audiograms.
To measure the tinnitus's impact on the person, the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory, or THI, was used.
The THI has twenty-five questions; yes scores four, sometimes two, no zero, and the total ranges from zero to one hundred.
In the grading by McCombe and colleagues, thirty-eight to fifty-six points is a moderate handicap.
In our case the total score is forty-eight; so it is moderate.
The questions with high scores point to areas to address first in counseling, such as sleep and anxiety.
The scale does not make a diagnosis; it shows how much the tinnitus affects the person and how this changes over follow-up.
Tinnitus often comes with oversensitivity to everyday sounds, or hyperacusis; so it is asked about separately.
The person says sounds such as clattering plates and slamming doors have become unpleasant in recent months.
This complaint can also be recorded as a number with a short hyperacusis questionnaire.
When loudness discomfort levels were measured, values were slightly below those commonly seen in people with normal hearing.
To avoid discomfort, the person has started wearing earplugs even in quiet places; we discuss this, as the habit can increase sensitivity.
Counseling starts with information: findings are explained clearly, and we explain that tinnitus is a condition many people have.
We discuss that ringing is usually not a sign of a dangerous disease, but may be a warning to protect the ears.
To avoid silence, sound enrichment such as a fan or nature sounds at night is suggested.
We explain using hearing protection at concerts, and limiting volume and duration when listening through headphones.
The person is referred for an ENT assessment.
If distress is marked, referral for cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT, the approach with the strongest evidence, is discussed.
After a few months, the THI and measurements are repeated to track change.

sahneler.metin: A normal audiogram does not show that tinnitus is not real. Show the findings, take the worry seriously, and refer without delay in severe distress.
cumleler: A clinical tip: a sentence like "your audiogram is normal, nothing is wrong" raises the person's worry and shakes their trust.
Instead, show the extended high-frequency and OAE findings and explain that the tinnitus may have an explanation.
Take sleep problems and anxiety seriously.
With severe anxiety, signs of depression or thoughts of self-harm, refer the person to a physician and mental health support without delay.
The audiologist gives no advice on drugs or supplements suggested for tinnitus; these questions go to the physician.
This chart shows how the THI score of the person in our case changes over time.
The score, forty-eight at baseline, falls to twenty-eight after three months of counseling and sound enrichment.
This twenty-point drop reaches the difference of about twenty points that test-retest studies consider meaningful.
The person now says they fall asleep more easily and notice the ringing less.
Extended high-frequency thresholds are also repeated at follow-up, since this region can be thought of as the cochlea's early warning zone.

maddeler.metin: Standard audiogram normal in both ears
DPOAE low amplitude in the highs

cumleler: Pure-tone: normal hearing thresholds in both ears from two hundred fifty to eight thousand hertz; speech scores one hundred percent.
Extended high frequencies: raised thresholds in both ears from ten thousand hertz up, no response at sixteen thousand hertz.
OAE: low DPOAE amplitudes from four to eight thousand hertz; a mild SNR loss on the QuickSIN.
Scales: THI forty-eight, moderate; hyperacusis complaint present.
Advice: ENT assessment, tinnitus counseling, safe listening and a check in three months.

maddeler.metin: A normal audiogram may not explain tinnitus
Above 8 kHz and OAEs add information
THI and hyperacusis questions guide the plan

cumleler: A normal audiogram does not mean the tinnitus is not real; it shows only two hundred fifty to eight thousand hertz.
Extended high-frequency audiometry and OAEs can show changes the standard audiogram cannot see.
The THI and hyperacusis questions put numbers on the impact of tinnitus and set the priorities for counseling.
The plan consists of information, sound enrichment, safe listening, referral if needed, and follow-up.

sahneler.soru: A THI score of 48. What grade?
sahneler.aciklama: In the McCombe grading, _38 to 56_ points is moderate.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: what grade is a person who scores forty-eight points on the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: moderate.
In the McCombe grading, scores from thirty-eight to fifty-six are read as a moderate handicap.
